title: How to Ask for Help So It's Easy to Say Yes
summary: People agree to help more often than we expect. How to package a clear ask, who to ask, and how to help a teammate without taking over their keyboard.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Your coffee went cold forty minutes ago. The same test is still red, the cursor hasn't moved, and nothing is on fire. No outage, no deadline today, and nobody even knows you're stuck. There's just the small private pressure of standing still while the rest of the team seems to keep moving.

You know you could ask someone. You also have a list of reasons not to: they're busy, it's probably something obvious, and you'd like to show you can carry your own work. Most of those reasons don't hold up, and the ones that do have a fix.

Ask, and people usually help

In 2008, Francis Flynn and Vanessa Bohns ran six studies on what happens when people ask others for help directly (If You Need Help, Just Ask). In the first three, help seekers underestimated how many people would agree by as much as 50%, in the lab and in field settings. The gap came from what each side pays attention to. The person asking focuses on the cost of saying yes. The person being asked feels the social cost of saying no.

Those were mostly strangers asked for small favors. Keep that number in mind the next time you assume a teammate will be annoyed.

The second worry is that asking makes you look less capable. Alison Wood Brooks, Francesca Gino and Maurice Schweitzer tested exactly that in a set of experiments published in Management Science in 2015, and found people rated advice seekers as more competent than people who didn't ask (Smart People Ask for (My) Advice). The effect was strongest when the task was hard, when the person was asked for advice personally, and when they actually had expertise. On easy tasks, asking neither helped nor hurt, and asking someone with no relevant expertise could backfire (MIT Sloan Management Review). So ask, and ask someone who'd actually know.

Package the ask

Most help requests stall at the first message, because the helper has to rebuild the whole story before they can start thinking. Simon Tatham's classic essay on bug reports gives you the shape. If you can, let the other person see the failure with their own eyes. If you can't, describe it in detail: "State what you saw, and also state what you expected to see" (How to Report Bugs Effectively). A good ask to a teammate has the same bones:

  • What you're trying to do, in one sentence.
  • What you expected, and what happened instead, with the exact error.
  • What you've already checked, so nobody repeats it.
  • The smallest thing that reproduces it: a failing test, a curl command, a branch name.
  • The kind of help you want: a second pair of eyes, a pointer to the right person, or 15 minutes on a call.

Here's the difference in practice. "Hey, got a sec? The payment test is broken" means the helper starts from zero. Compare: "I'm adding partial refunds to the payment service. test_refund_partial fails with a 409 from the ledger mock, and I expected a 200. I've checked the fixture and the mock config. Branch is refund-partial. Could you look for 10 minutes this afternoon? I think I'm missing something about how the mock handles idempotency keys."

The second message takes two extra minutes to write. Fairly often you spot the bug halfway through writing it, and then you don't need to send it at all.

Say what you already understand

Julia Evans, who writes some of the clearest technical explainers around, has a simple trick in How to Ask Good Questions: state what you understand so far, then ask "is that right?" It shows exactly where your mental model goes wrong, so the other person can fix that one spot instead of explaining everything. She also likes questions whose answer is a plain fact, and she thinks about who to ask: whether it's a good time for them, and whether someone a little less senior could answer just as well, which spreads the load.

When you're the one being asked

How you answer decides whether people ask again. If the first response is a sigh, people learn to hide. If it's a takeover, they learn to stop thinking. Good help is often smaller than you'd expect: a question that narrows the search, a quick sketch of the flow, or "I've hit this before, look at how the mock stores keys," and then letting them finish the fix.

Senior engineers shape this more than they realize. When a senior says "I'm not sure yet, can you look at this with me?", everyone else gets permission to be honest sooner. Evans has advice for this side too: answer the questions you know how to answer. It helps the person asking, and it locks in what you've learned.

Keep what you learned

A good ask leaves something behind. The confusion a new hire hits becomes a line in the onboarding doc. The debugging path you've now walked twice becomes a checklist. The awkward spot in the architecture becomes a refactor ticket. One person's stuck afternoon ends up making the next person's afternoon shorter.

This post is about how to ask. If your trouble is mostly when to ask, the companion post on asking for help early covers the timing side.

Try this week

  • The next time you're stuck for half an hour, write the five-line ask above, even if you end up not sending it.
  • Add a "what I've tried" line to your team's help-channel template.
  • When someone asks you for help, ask them one question before you touch the keyboard.
  • If you're senior, ask one question in public that you genuinely don't know the answer to.

faqs.q: Does asking for help at work make you look incompetent?
faqs.a: Research suggests the opposite. Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer (Management Science, 2015) found people rated those who asked them for advice as more competent, especially on hard tasks and when the person asked had real expertise. On easy tasks it neither helped nor hurt.

faqs.q: Will people actually help if I ask?
faqs.a: Usually more than you expect. In Flynn and Bohns' 2008 studies, people asking for help underestimated how many others would agree by as much as 50%. Askers focus on the cost of saying yes, while the people being asked feel how awkward it is to say no.

faqs.q: What should a good help request include?
faqs.a: What you're trying to do, what you expected versus what happened (with the exact error), what you've already checked, the smallest way to reproduce it, and what kind of help you want, such as a quick look or a 15-minute call.

faqs.q: How do I help a teammate without taking over?
faqs.a: Start with a question that narrows the search, sketch the flow together, or point at the trap you've hit before, then let them finish the fix. Taking the keyboard solves today's problem but teaches people to stop thinking or stop asking.

faqs.q: Who should I ask for help?
faqs.a: Someone who actually knows the area, since asking a non-expert can backfire. Check whether it's a good time for them, and consider someone slightly less senior who still knows the answer so the same person isn't asked every time.
